In the CSL theory, as in the SL theory which inspired it, the reduction of a wave function for a macroscopic (many-particle) object proceeds at a faster rate than for a single particle. (This is at the heart of the resolution of the trigger problem.) The many-particle theory has other interesting features not encountered when dealing with single particle behavior. We do not discuss these features here; they are treated in Ref. 12. Our aim here has been to provide enough information to facilitate understanding of these and other problems in the CSL theory via path integrals.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>This chapter introduces the two equations that completely define CSL, for the simplest case, that is, a state vector in a two-dimensional Hilbert space. One equation is the modified evolution equation for the state vector which depends upon a Brownian motion function of time, B(t), a Hermitian operator A called the “collapse-generating operator,” and a collapse rate parameter λ. The state vector evolution is linear, but not unitary, so its norm changes with time. The second equation is called the probability rule. It says the probability a particular B(t) occurs in Nature is proportional to the squared norm of the state vector, that is, high norm state vectors are most likely to occur. The chapter shows how an initial state vector that is a superposition of the eigenstates of A evolves to one eigenstate, with the Born probability, as predicted by standard quantum theory. Finally, it discusses the density matrix description of the ensemble of evolutions under all possible B(t).</jats:p>
